sources.title: 68% of the world population projected to live in urban areas by 2050, says UN (2018 Revision of World Urbanization Prospects)
State of World Population 2007: Unleashing the Potential of Urban Growth

sources.publisher: United Nations, Department of Economic and Social Affairs
sources.title: Goal 11: Make cities and human settlements inclusive, safe, resilient and sustainable

facts.text: Each country's statistics office decides what counts as an urban area, so definitions differ between countries.
The urban shares are collected and smoothed by the UN Population Division for its World Urbanization Prospects.
In the World Bank series, 34.2 percent of the world's people lived in urban areas in 1960 and 57.6 percent in 2024.
In the World Bank series, the world's urban share passed 50 percent between 2006 (49.9) and 2007 (50.4).
In 2007, about 3.40 billion people lived in urban areas and 3.34 billion in rural areas, the first year the urban total was larger.
A UN population report published in 2007 announced that in 2008, for the first time, more than half of humanity, about 3.3 billion people, would live in urban areas.
The same report projected that towns and cities would hold almost 5 billion people by 2030.
The world's urban population rose from about 1.03 billion in 1960 to about 4.69 billion in 2024, more than four times as many.
According to the UN, the urban population grew from 751 million in 1950 to 4.2 billion in 2018.
The UN projected in 2018 that 68 percent of the world's people would live in urban areas by 2050.
The UN expected close to 90 percent of the urban growth up to 2050 to take place in Asia and Africa.
In 2018 the most urbanized regions were Northern America (82 percent), Latin America and the Caribbean (81 percent) and Europe (74 percent); Africa was 43 percent.
Close to half of the world's urban dwellers live in towns and cities with fewer than 500,000 people.
In 2018 there were 33 megacities of over 10 million people, and the UN expected 43 by 2030.
East Asia and the Pacific stayed at about 24.9 percent urban from 1960 to 1970, then climbed to 62.4 percent in 2020.
East Asia and the Pacific passed the 50 percent mark in 2008 (50.2), one year after the world as a whole.
Sub-Saharan Africa's urban share rose from 14.3 percent in 1960 to 42.2 percent in 2020, nearly three times as high.
In 2024 Sub-Saharan Africa had about 570 million urban and 720 million rural residents, so most people there still lived in the countryside.
Europe and Central Asia was already 55.0 percent urban in 1960 and reached 73.5 percent in 2020, the highest of the regions shown.
Derived: from 1960 to 2020 the urban share rose about 37.5 points in East Asia and the Pacific, 27.8 in Sub-Saharan Africa, 22.2 for the world and 18.5 in Europe and Central Asia.
Derived: Europe and Central Asia rose 12.4 points from 1960 to 1990 but only 6.1 points from 1990 to 2020.
SDG 11 aims to make cities and human settlements inclusive, safe, resilient and sustainable; target 11.1 calls for adequate, safe and affordable housing for all and upgraded slums by 2030.
About 1.12 billion people, close to one in four urban residents, lived in slums or informal settlements in 2022.
